html_en:
As AI agents mature from coding assistants to enterprise-grade automation, a new technical discipline is emerging — and the infrastructure to support it is evolving rapidly.

The Rise of AI Automation Engineers

The AI industry is witnessing the birth of a new professional category. Aaron Levie, CEO of Box, articulated this shift perfectly in a detailed thread about enterprise AI adoption:
"As advanced agents move from coding to the rest of knowledge work, it takes a real amount of work and know-how to get right. You need to ensure agents have the right context and data to work with, wire up systems to agents in a safe and secure way, ensure that the agents are producing quality output, design the end-state workflow where and how humans will be in the loop, maintain the agents when there are model and system upgrades, and more."
Levie's observation that "this isn't a side project or something you can just do on nights and weekends" highlights a crucial industry inflection point. Companies like Box are now hiring dedicated AI automation engineers — "a highly technical role that will partner with the business directly and help augment how they work." This isn't theoretical anymore. Dan Shipper demonstrated this hands-on approach with a weekend hack project that took just five minutes: connecting a MIDI keyboard to create chord-recognition exercises using AI. "literally 5 minutes start to finish, and it works flawlessly," he noted.

Infrastructure Reality Check: The Scale Behind the Magic

While consumer-facing AI tools capture headlines, the infrastructure layer is experiencing explosive growth. Watch/Listen: No Priors episode with Baseten CEO Tuhin Srivastava provided crucial insights into the AI inference market's unprecedented expansion.
"We've grown 30x over the last year... what's happened over the last twenty four months is that everyone is realizing that you can put AI everywhere. The open source models have crossed some sort of chasm in terms of their baseline capability."
Srivastava's revelation that 99% of inference demand still comes from AI-native companies, not enterprises, suggests we're still in the early innings. "The majority of the market hasn't come online and added AI into their systems," he observed. This creates a fascinating paradox: massive growth happening primarily within a small subset of early adopters. The infrastructure demands are creating interesting technical challenges. Anthropic's new blog post on Managed Agents reveals how they're solving scalability through classical systems design principles, "virtualizing the components of an agent" much like operating systems virtualized hardware decades ago.

The Practical AI Revolution

Beyond enterprise automation, AI is solving refreshingly mundane problems. Peter Yang captured this beautifully with a simple wish: "When I receive those 10 page weekly newsletters from my kid's school I want AI to tell me if there's early dismissal or anything I should pay attention to." This practical approach extends to developer tooling. Stefan Petri shared how he's building custom tools for efficiency: challenging Codex to improve test endpoints and creating systems that can search through his complete Twitter archive. "You gotta build yourself the tools to work more efficient," he noted.

Model Naming and Market Dynamics

Even OpenAI's Sam Altman is feeling the pressure from the community's model naming preferences. His playful tweet about naming the next model "goblin" — "almost worth it to make you all happy..." — garnered over 9,000 likes, suggesting the community's voice carries real weight in product decisions. Meanwhile, the technical community continues pushing boundaries. A fascinating development emerged when someone attempted rewriting Bun in Rust, achieving 99.8% test suite compatibility — prompting the observation that "we're not being ambitious enough."
The day's conversations reveal an industry transitioning from experimental AI to production-grade automation systems. While infrastructure scales exponentially behind the scenes, the real magic happens in the practical applications — from parsing school newsletters to building weekend MIDI projects. The future belongs to those who can bridge the gap between AI's raw capabilities and real-world workflows.
html_zh:
今日AI行业的核心主题围绕着代理自动化工程师这一新兴职业的出现，以及开发者们正在构建更智能、更实用的AI工具。从管理层到工程师，每个人都在探索如何让AI真正融入日常工作流程。

代理自动化工程师：AI时代的新职业

Aaron Levie预测了一个引人注目的职业趋势。Box的CEO在推特上详细描述了他们正在招聘的"AI自动化工程师"角色：
"当高级代理从编程扩展到其他知识工作时，需要真正的工作量和专业知识才能做好。你需要确保代理拥有正确的上下文和数据来工作，以安全可靠的方式将系统连接到代理，确保代理产生高质量的输出，设计人类参与循环的端到端工作流程，在模型和系统升级时维护代理等等。这不是副业项目或你可以在晚上和周末做的事情。你需要设计和开发将在关键任务工作流程中使用的强大代理。这是一个高度技术性的工作，非常类似于内部功能的前置部署工程师。"
这一观点呼应了当前业界的一个重要趋势：AI代理不再是实验性工具，而是需要专业工程师来构建和维护的企业基础设施。Levie表示，他预计未来大多数公司都会有这类角色的多种变体。

实用AI工具的兴起

开发者社区正在构建解决日常痛点的AI应用。Peter Yang分享了一个许多家长都能共鸣的需求：
"你知道什么会是一个很好的AI自动化吗：当我收到孩子学校那些10页的周刊时，我希望AI告诉我是否有提前放学或任何我应该注意的事情。"
与此同时，Dan Shipper展示了AI工具开发的惊人速度。他描述了一个周末黑客项目："嘿codex，制作一个监听脚本和一个小型web应用来显示我正在弹奏的和弦"，整个过程从开始到完成只用了5分钟，并且运行完美。

基础设施的规模化挑战

在No Priors播客中，Baseten CEO Tuhin Srivastava揭示了AI推理市场的惊人增长：
"过去一年我们增长了30倍...我认为每个人都意识到你可以把AI放在任何地方。你有从闭源到开源模型的所有这些很好的选择。开源模型在基线能力方面已经跨越了某种鸿沟。"
Srivastava强调了应用层存在的关键原因：公司拥有只有他们能收集到的独特用户信号。以医疗转录公司Abridge为例，他解释道这种深度集成和专有数据访问权限使得前沿模型公司难以简单地"吞噬"这些专业化应用。

工程创新与工具改进

Anthropic发布了关于扩展托管代理的重要技术博客，提出了"将大脑与手分离"的架构理念：
"我们得出的解决方案是将我们认为的'大脑'（Claude和其工具）从'手'（沙盒和执行动作的工具）以及'会话'（会话事件日志）中解耦出来。每个都成为一个对其他组件假设很少的接口，每个都可以独立失败或被替换。"
这种架构改进解决了一个古老的计算问题：如何为"尚未想到的程序"设计系统。 个人开发者也在推动边界。Stefan Petre展示了一个有趣的应用："Birdclaw有我完整的推特存档，所以我可以要求Codex找到我曾经收藏或书签的任何古怪推文"。
轻松的一面：Sam Altman在推特上开玩笑说要将下一个模型命名为"goblin"，"几乎值得让你们所有人开心"，这条推文获得了9000多个赞，显示了社区对更富有个性的AI命名的渴望。
